title: Why Does Bread Taste Better at 140°C? 🍞
description:
Why does toast turn brown and taste better than bread? In a toaster, dry heat starts the Maillard reaction between sugars and amino acids, building hundreds of new flavor molecules and brown melanoidins.

topic: Why does toast turn brown and taste better?
script: You just ate molecules, your bread never had. That's what toast is. So why does it taste so much better? Bread holds two key ingredients: sugars, and amino acids, the building blocks of protein. Normally, they mostly ignore each other. But in the toaster, dry heat drives water out of the surface. Then, at around a hundred and forty degrees Celsius, they start reacting. It's called the Maillard reaction, first described in nineteen twelve. It builds hundreds of new flavor molecules, nutty, roasty, toasty. And the brown? That's melanoidins, big brown molecules. The inside stays cooler and wetter, so it stays soft and pale. Push it too far, though, and it burns to bitter black char. So what's your perfect toast: pale gold, or nearly burned?
key_facts: The Maillard reaction is between amino acids and reducing sugars and typically proceeds rapidly from around 140 to 165 C (Wikipedia)
Louis Camille Maillard first described it in 1912 (Wikipedia, Chemistry World)
It can produce hundreds of different flavor compounds (Wikipedia, Science ABC)
Melanoidins are the brown molecules; dry heat drives off the bread's water, and excess water slows or halts browning (Science ABC)
